## Time Value of Money

In finance you never do anything for free and you would always prefer to have
money now rather than later. For example, if you loan someone money, you
expect to be compensated for giving up the opportunity to use that money for
some other purpose. This is the **time value of money** and the compensation
is called **interest**.

:::{.definition data-title="Interest"}
**Interest** is the cost of borrowing money or the return on investment for
lending money. It is typically expressed as a percentage of the principal
amount over a specified period of time.
:::

Suppose we loan an initial amount (the **principal**) $P$ to a borrower for
some period of time. To compensate us for the use of our money, the borrower
agrees to pay interest at an agreed rate. Interest **accrues** as it is earned
and is added to the principal. The total amount owed at the end of the loan
is called the **future value** $F$.

How much interest is earned depends on the periodic rate $r$, the number of
periods $m$ (determined by the loan duration and the payment frequency), and
whether the interest is **simple** or **compound**.

Throughout, $r$ is the rate per period (the effective annual rate when the
period is one year), $m$ is the number of periods (the number of compounding
periods per year when we work over one year), $r^{(m)}$ is a nominal annual
rate compounded $m$ times per year, $\delta$ is the continuously compounded
rate and $t$ is measured in years.

## Simple vs Compound Interest

In **simple interest**, the interest is calculated only on the principal

$$
F_s = P(1 + rm).
$$

:::{.definition data-title="Compound Interest"}

In **compound interest**, the interest is calculated on the accrued total
(principal plus interest)

$$
F_c = P(1 + r)^m.
$$

:::

:::{.example data-title="Simple vs Compound Interest"}

Suppose we loan $P=\$100$ at a monthly interest rate of $r=1.5\%$ for $m=12$
months. The future value of the loan under simple and compound interest is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_s & = 100(1 + 0.015 \cdot 12) = 100(1.18) = \$118 \\
F_c & = 100(1 + 0.015)^{12} \approx 100(1.195618) \approx \$119.56.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

## Present Value and Discounting

Compounding runs in reverse to give the **present value** of an amount $F$
received after $m$ periods. Solving $F = P(1+r)^m$ for $P$,

$$
P = F(1+r)^{-m} = F\,v^m, \qquad v = \frac{1}{1+r},
$$

where $v$ is the **discount factor** for one period. Discounting is the same
operation as compounding with the time direction reversed.

The **effective discount rate** is the interest paid in advance, per unit of
the amount received at the end of the year,

$$
d = 1 - v = \frac{r}{1+r}.
$$

:::{.example data-title="Present Value"}

The present value of $\$1000$ received in 5 years at an effective annual rate
of $8\%$ is $1000(1.08)^{-5} \approx \$680.58$.

:::

In [[interest-rates]] the discount factor over $[t,T]$ becomes the
zero-coupon bond price $p(t,T)$, which allows the rate to vary with time.

## Annualization

In finance, interest rates are often expressed on an annual basis, even if the
interest is compounded more frequently.

:::{.definition data-title="Nominal Interest Rate"}

The nominal rate $r^{(m)}$ is a stated annual rate that is *compounded $m$
times per year*. It is quoted as a yearly figure, but interest is actually
credited every $1/m$ of a year at the periodic rate $r^{(m)}/m$.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Effective Interest Rate"}

The effective annual rate $r$ is the single once-a-year rate that produces
the same growth as the nominal rate over one year. Since $1$ dollar grows to
$\left(1+\frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m$ after one year with $m$ compounding
periods,

$$
1 + r = \left(1 + \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r = \left(1 + \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m - 1.
$$

:::

In North American consumer finance, the effective annual rate is called APY
(annual percentage yield) for savings. The nominal rate on loans is called APR
(annual percentage rate), which is usually just the periodic rate times the
number of periods, so it understates the true cost relative to the effective
rate. The process of converting a nominal rate to an effective annual rate is
called **annualization**. Its main purpose is to provide a standardized way to
compare interest rates across different financial products and investment
opportunities, so that investors and borrowers can see the true cost or return
of a product over a one-year period.

:::{.example data-title="Annualization"}

Suppose we take out a loan with a nominal interest rate of $r^{(12)} = 6\%$
compounded monthly. The effective annual rate is

$$
r = \left(1 + \frac{0.06}{12}\right)^{12} - 1
\approx 1.061678 - 1 \approx 6.17\%.
$$

:::

To compare two nominal rates with different compounding frequencies, convert
through the effective rate. Equating $1 + r$ for frequencies $m$ and $k$ gives

$$
r^{(k)} = k\left[\left(1 + \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^{m/k} - 1\right].
$$

For example, $r^{(12)} = 6\%$ is equivalent to
$r^{(2)} = 2\left[(1.005)^6 - 1\right] \approx 6.08\%$ compounded
semi-annually.

## Continuous Compounding

Continuous compounding is the limit of the nominal-rate setup as the number
of compounding periods per year $m \to \infty$. Interest is effectively
credited over infinitesimally small periods, and the effective annual rate
approaches an upper limit of $e^r - 1$.

Start with the future value after $t$ years at nominal rate $r$ compounded
$m$ times per year, $F = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^{mt}$, and take logs

$$
\ln\frac{F}{P} = mt\,\ln\!\left(1+\frac{r}{m}\right)
\;\xrightarrow{\,m\to\infty\,}\; rt,
$$

since $\ln(1+x) \sim x$ as $x \to 0$. Exponentiating gives

$$
F = P\,e^{rt}.
$$

One can reach the same result by applying L'Hopital's rule to the logarithm
of the growth factor. There is no $m$ in the formula: a common error is to
carry $m$ into the continuous formula, but $e^{rt}$ already accounts for
infinitely frequent compounding.

In actuarial notation, the continuously compounded rate is called the
**force of interest** $\delta$. The accumulation function is
$a(t) = e^{\int_0^t \delta(s)\,ds}$, which reduces to $e^{\delta t}$ when
$\delta$ is constant. Equivalently, $\delta$ is the logarithmic derivative
of the accumulation function

$$
\delta(t) = \frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}.
$$

When the force of interest varies in time it is called the short rate in
[[interest-rates]]. With a constant force of interest,

$$
1 + r = e^{\delta}, \qquad \delta = \ln(1+r),
\qquad \delta = \lim_{m\to\infty} r^{(m)}.
$$

The force of interest is below the effective annual rate but above the
effective discount rate $d$. In terms of the nominal rates from before,
$r^{(m)}$ decreases toward $\delta$ as $m$ grows

$$
r = r^{(1)} > r^{(2)} > r^{(4)} > r^{(12)} > \cdots > \delta > d.
$$

Converting a continuous rate to an effective annual rate (APY) is just
$e^{r}-1$. At $r = 6\%$ this gives about $6.184\%$. Take a $12\%$ nominal
rate:

| Compounding | Effective annual rate |
| - | - |
| Annual ($m=1$) | $12.000\%$ |
| Monthly ($m=12$) | $12.683\%$ |
| Daily ($m=365$) | $12.747\%$ |
| Continuous ($m\to\infty$) | $e^{0.12}-1 \approx 12.750\%$ |

Most of the gain from more frequent compounding comes by $m=12$. On a
deposit of $\$1000$ for one year, daily and continuous compounding differ by
about three cents (\$1127.47 against \$1127.50), so continuous compounding is
used mainly for mathematical convenience.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Effective annual rate against compounding frequency (12% nominal)."

library(ggplot2)

nominal <- 0.12
df <- data.frame(m = 1:365)
df$effective <- (1 + nominal / df$m)^df$m - 1

ggplot(df, aes(x = m, y = effective)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = exp(nominal) - 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "Compounding periods per year (m)", y = "Effective annual rate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

:::{.example data-title="Continuous Compounding"}

Investing $\$1000$ at $8\%$ for 5 years gives
$1000\,e^{0.4} \approx \$1491.82$ under continuous compounding, versus
$\$1469.33$ with annual compounding.

To find a doubling time, solve $e^{\delta t} = 2$

$$
t = \frac{\ln 2}{\delta}.
$$

Since $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$, a rate of $R\%$ doubles money in roughly $70/R$
years. For annually compounded rates the **rule of 72**, $t \approx 72/R$, is
more accurate: at $6\%$ it gives $12$ years against an exact value of
$\ln 2 / \ln 1.06 \approx 11.90$.

:::

## Day-Count Conventions

The year fraction $t$ used in practice depends on a market convention, so the
same quoted rate can accrue slightly different amounts of interest. Common
choices are

- **Actual/365**: actual days elapsed divided by $365$.
- **Actual/360**: actual days elapsed divided by $360$, common for money
  markets and LIBOR.
- **30/360**: each month is treated as $30$ days and each year as $360$ days,
  common for bonds.
